clinicalPearls: An X-linked disorder chiefly of males combining short stature with characteristic facial, limb and genital features
Facial features include hypertelorism, a broad forehead, a short nose with anteverted nares, and a widow's peak
The genital hallmark is a shawl scrotum, in which scrotal folds surround the base of the penis
Hand findings include short broad hands with brachydactyly, clinodactyly and characteristic interdigital webbing
Intellectual ability is often normal or only mildly affected, distinguishing it from many other X-linked syndromes
Caused by variants in FGD1, encoding a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor that activates the Rho-family GTPase Cdc42
Carrier females may show subtle features such as mild hypertelorism
reference.pathophysiology: FGD1 encodes a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor that specifically activates the Rho-family small GTPase Cdc42, a key regulator of the actin cytoskeleton, cell shape and signalling during skeletal and craniofacial development. Loss-of-function variants impair Cdc42 activation, disturbing the cytoskeletal and signalling processes that guide bone growth and morphogenesis, producing the short stature and the facial, limb and genital anomalies. As an X-linked gene, males are predominantly affected while carrier females may show only mild features. Cognition is frequently spared because the developmental effect is weighted toward skeletal and connective-tissue patterning.
additionalInvestigations: Growth assessment and, where indicated, evaluation of the growth axis
Skeletal and hand imaging for brachydactyly and vertebral anomalies
Ophthalmological review for associated eye findings
Targeted FGD1 sequencing or a gene panel or exome sequencing
redFlags: Cervical spine instability (odontoid anomaly) posing a risk during anaesthesia or trauma
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have a good outlook with generally normal or near-normal intellect and manageable skeletal and genital features; short stature persists but adult function is usually good. Care focuses on growth, orthopaedic and genital issues.
pitfalls: Confusing the phenotype with Noonan syndrome and missing FGD1 testing
Overlooking possible cervical spine instability before anaesthesia
Assuming intellectual disability is invariable and mislabelling the child
Missing subtle features in carrier females
management: Monitor growth longitudinally and evaluate the growth-hormone axis where short stature is marked, referring to paediatric endocrinology as indicated
Provide orthopaedic assessment and management of skeletal anomalies including brachydactyly, joint laxity and cervical-spine or vertebral anomalies
Arrange surgical correction of genital and inguinal anomalies such as cryptorchidism and inguinal hernia, with dental and orthodontic care for malocclusion
Undertake ophthalmological review for associated ocular features such as hypertelorism, strabismus and refractive error
Offer developmental and educational support where any learning or attention difficulty is identified, though intellect is usually normal
Provide genetic counselling for this X-linked FGD1 condition, including carrier assessment of the mother and family
Coordinate long-term care through clinical genetics and paediatric multidisciplinary services
